https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/08/12/pak.text: Menü Kereső Kiemelt beruházássá nyilvánította a kormány a paksi atomerőmű miatt szükséges dunai munkálatokat Gazdaság Belföld Előd Fruzsina Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kiemelt beruházások lesznek a paksi atomerőmű alacsony vízállás miatt kellő mederberuházásai, az ezekhez kapcsolódó közigazgatási hatósági ügyek pedig kiemelt jelentőségű ügyek – derül ki a Magyar Közlöny szerdai számából. A rendelet szövege szerint a kormány célja a Duna medrében elhelyezkedő fenékküszöb soron kívüli megtervezése és megvalósítása a paksi atomerőmű üzembiztonságának minden körülmények közötti fenntartása érdekében. A kormányrendelet a Magyar Péter miniszterelnök által néhány órával ezelőtt bejelentett lépésekhez kapcsolódik. A kormány szerdán döntött arról, hogy fenékküszöbbel, annak kiépítéséig két elsüllyeszthető bárkával gondoskodnak a Duna elégséges szintű mélységéről Paksnál az alacsony vízállás idején. Az erőműnél idén nyáron fellépett energiakrízis hátteréről, az ide vezető mulasztásokról itt írtunk részletesen. A kiemelt beruházásoknál a közbeszerzési eljárások egyszerűsített formában, indokolás nélkül folytathatók le, a szükséges közigazgatási eljárások ügyintézési határideje általában 15 nap, szakhatósági eljárásoké 8 nap, a kapcsolódó közterület-használat díjmentes, külön engedély nélkül 6 hónapig lehetséges. A paksi mederberuházásoknál a rendelet szerint a környezetvédelmi működési engedélyt 2026. szeptember 30-ig kell kérelmezni. A vízjogi létesítési engedély megszerzése alól a beruházás mentesül, de 2026. október 15-ig fennmaradási engedélyt kell kérni, vízgazdálkodási bírság nem szabható ki. A természetvédelmi engedélyezési eljárásokat 2026. október 15-ig kell megindítani, a fakivágási engedélykérelmet szintén ugyaneddig kell benyújtani, természetvédelmi bírság nem szabható ki. https://finance.yahoo.com/small-business.text: Oops, something went wrong U.S. markets closed Baltics transform from Soviet stagnation to startup hubs Katarzyna SKIBA August 1, 2026 3 min read Rideshare service Bolt is one of several internationally recognised Baltic startups (Loic VENANCE) Stepping into the newly renovated Vilnius airport, visitors are greeted with a slew of billboards advertising products "Made in Lithuania", including cybersecurity giant NordVPN. Rather than focusing on heritage or artisanal craftsmanship promoted in similar campaigns in Italy or France, Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours Estonia and Latvia are highlighting they are home to innovation. The three countries have a growing number of startups recognised worldwide, such as online reselling platform Vinted, rideshare service Bolt and videotelephony pioneer Skype. Despite a total population of just over six million people, the Baltic states possessed around 33,000 startups last year, according to data from Lursoft IT, a Latvian company specialising in business and financial databases. They raised 20 percent more in funding in 2025 at 607 million euros ($700 million), according to Practica Capital and Firstpick's annual report on the sector. The Baltic states now have 17 "unicorns" -- startups with a valuation above $1.0 billion. - 'Entrepreneurial spirit' - Fewer than four decades ago Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania regained their independence but inherited inefficient factories from the Soviet Union's command economy. "Regaining independence... unlocked the entrepreneurial spirit previously suppressed under Soviet rule," said Latvian-American entrepreneur Girts Graudins, who noted that the region has a history as a science and manufacturing hub going back to the turn of the 20th century. The ruins of the Soviet command economy were also a crucible for innovation, said Kadri Ukrainski, who lectures on the subject at Estonia's Tartu University. "Coming from (the) Soviet times, we didn't have very good telephone systems," she said, leading to the creation of Skype -- Estonia's first, and arguably its most famous, unicorn. The app helped the once-behind country leap forward, she argued, "helping us to solve this very backward communication system". Founded in 2003 by a couple of Scandinavian entrepreneurs along with four Estonian developers, Skype had 50 million registered users worldwide by 2005, when it was sold to online auction site eBay for approximately $2.6 billion. European Union accession in 2004 also brought the Baltic states access to European markets. Estonia, with a population of 1.3 million, now has 10 active unicorns -- the most per capita in Europe. - Startup 'multiplier effect' - Although Skype is now defunct -- retired last year by Microsoft which bought the app in 2011, its legacy as the first Baltic unicorn can still be felt across the region. Story Continues Known as the "Skype mafia" effect, founders and early employees took the experience they gained from the company and went on to start their own companies, inspiring others to do the same. Lithuania's first unicorn, second-hand clothing platform Vinted, has had a similar impact. "Vinted's journey has certainly been intertwined with the broader development of Lithuania's startup ecosystem," said the company's vice president for corporate affairs, Jessie de la Merced, arguing that its presence has had a "multiplier effect". Vinted, which became a unicorn in 2019, reached $8 billion in market valuation in April, and Lithuania now boasts a total of six unicorns. Unicorns' effects can also be felt across the local economy, said Karolina Urbonaite, the head of Startup Lithuania, a government institution which supports the country's startup ecosystem. "Our startups pay a lot of taxes. They create new jobs," she said, adding that Lithuanian startups employed over 20,000 people in total, paying high salaries and attracting foreign investment to the country. A heavy focus on STEM education (Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics) in the Baltics is also helping forge the next generation of fintech entrepreneurs. Baltic STEM students rank higher than those from France, Sweden, the United States and Norway in the OECD's latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). There has also been a change of aspirations. "Before, the role models were artists and musicians," said Ronny Eriksson, founder of entrepreneurship studio New Nordic Way in Finland. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn9n.text: Image caption, Many of the soldiers were born in Ukraine but consider themselves to be Russian By Sarah Rainsford ,Â Southern and Eastern Europe correspondentÂ Â and Â with reporting by Mariana MatveichukÂ ,Â Reporting from Western Ukraine Published 1 hour ago In Western Ukraine, behind high walls and layers of locked gates, there is a camp full of men captured fighting for Russia. Many of those crouching in the shade around the edges of the prison yard were recruited from big cities like St Petersburg and Yekaterinburg, not far-flung and poorer regions like at the start of the full-scale invasion. But not all the prisoners are Russian. Amongst them are soldiers from Ukraine itself: the men who went to war with their own country. Interviewing prisoners of war is not straightforward: to be sure they are not being coerced, first and foremost, and then to assess how openly they are speaking in the circumstances. But with no access to the military inside Russia, it is a chance to assess the dynamics of this war and explore what might motivate the men fighting it. That includes the Ukrainian-born soldiers, on Russia's side. We gave everyone the right to refuse an interview and spoke to those who agreed far away from any guards, and without cameras. As well as several formal interviews, I was able to talk to prisoners directly, in Russian, in several locations. Image caption, The PoW camp holds men who come from occupied eastern Ukraine as well as some of the big Russian cities Anton was 10 when his part of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region was taken over by forces loyal to Moscow. In 2022, when Vladimir Putin escalated to all-out war, he turned 18 and signed up to fight immediately - for Russia. "I don't regret my choice. I went to defend my land," Anton insists and tells me his friends volunteered, too. "Then you get the SMS messages. Dead, dead, dead." Other prisoners say the same: that all those they went to war with have been killed. They also say fewer people are volunteering to replace them, despite enormous sign-up fees, which suggests Putin's desire to avoid mass mobilisation could soon be tested. When Ukraine captures its own citizens on the battlefield, they are put on trial for treason. But the men are then sent to PoW camps along with the Russians. Officially, Kyiv still sees them as Ukrainian and treats Russia's control of their regions as temporary. But the reality on the ground is more complex. "They're very pro-Russian, and their national identity is very blurred," is how Petro Yatsenko from Ukraine's coordination headquarters for PoWs puts it. Anton certainly does not class himself as a traitor. Image caption, This Christmas, shoppers may be buying decorations made by PoWs held in Ukraine "I consider myself Russian. A country means nothing, it's all about nationality. All my family are from Russia. All my roots are from there," he says. When we wonder about his Ukrainian surname, he brushes that off as irrelevant. An entire generation born in Ukraine has now grown up under occupation, with Russian schooling and media fully controlled by the Kremlin. Both have portrayed the authorities in Kyiv as "Nazis" and illegitimate for many years. Since the full-scale invasion, even more territory has been subjected to the same. Anton has absorbed it all and now speaks almost entirely in Russian slogans. He calls Putin "my President" and thinks he should push to take the rest of the Donbas, even though hundreds of thousands have already been killed trying. "It's a shame that people died, especially those who are innocent," Anton says. "But war is war. It could have been ended. But no-one wanted to do that." In the prison hospital, Artyom lies in a corner bed, his body full of shrapnel. He had only been fighting for two months. From Donetsk, like Anton, he also went to war willingly - not just for the cash. "We have our own grudges," Artyom says, recalling how his region came under heavy fire in 2014 as Ukrainian forces tried to stop it breaking away from Kyiv. But his military experience has left him bitter. His commander was "bad" and he never got any of his 400,000 rouble (Â£3,470; $5,000) sign-up fee. To add insult to Artyom's many injuries, the wounded Russian soldier in the bed opposite was paid five times as much. Image caption, Prisoners of war held by Ukraine work to earn money for better food and cigarettes. In this camp they are making coffins All the Ukrainian-born PoWs we interviewed came from areas occupied since 2014 and almost all joined the Russian army voluntarily. But one man from Donetsk region told us he had been forced to fight. His eyes darted around as he talked, unsure who he could trust. One official tally, citing "intelligence", suggests more than 50,000 Ukrainians have been conscripted against their will in occupied areas. Others put the figure far higher. This man told us that when the Russians invaded, his family had stayed, not through any political or national allegiance but because Donetsk was their home. Now, his only ambition was to get back to his wife and children, then avoid being returned to the front. "I'm just going to hide," he confided. Beneath the hospital windows and newly whitewashed walls there are rows of strawberries and cucumbers planted by the prisoners. Further on, the stench of varnish from an outhouse is overpowering. An official lifts a gold-coloured plastic handle from a bag near the door. "Guess what this is for?" he challenges us, grinning. Inside, I do a double-take: the men working inside are hammering together wooden coffins. I am told the last contract the prison got was for garden sheds. This one feels macabre. Across the courtyard in another workshop a handful of PoWs are making artificial Christmas trees, gaudy baubles strung from their machines. Like the coffin-makers, they tell me they use their wages to buy extra food and cigarettes. Sergei was born in the Ukrainian city of Luhansk but says he is Russian like his parents, who moved to the Donbas when both countries were part of the Soviet Union. He joined the Russian army a decade ago "to defend my homeland", but claims he will retire when he gets back, not return to the front. "I've done my bit." Most will have no choice. Stacking plastic branches next to Sergei is a drug dealer who signed up, like many, "exclusively" to avoid a long jail term. "For me, 15 years in prison was too much," Konstantin explains. "I know it probably doesn't excuse me, but it's a fact. I'm 44 now, I would be 60. So no." But Vshniki , or convict-soldiers, have to survive to the end of the war to be released and in the assault troops the odds are not good. Three convicted murderers told us they had thought they could walk free after fighting for a year, only to have their contacts renewed automatically. Image caption, While prisoners eat meals like this, a video plays in the background which debunks Russia's claim to Crimea When I ask about killing their fellow countrymen on the battlefield, Sergei calls the question "provocative" and does not want to answer. "I see nothing good in any war, and in a war like this there can be nothing good a priori ," Konstantin replies carefully. "I'm not saying we're the same as Ukrainians, but we are close. We all have relatives there. This just isn't good." He still thinks his decision to fight was right. Neither he nor Sergei expect the war to end soon. Both believe Putin won't stop until he controls the whole Donbas. "But everyone I know there has had enough," Konstantin says. "I just want this to be over, as soon as possible." At lunchtime, the prisoners in navy overalls file into the dining hall with heads bowed and hands clasped behind their backs. As they eat - soup and stew - a video called Myths about Crimea plays on a loop, demolishing Russia's claim to historic ownership of the peninsula that it stole from Ukraine in 2014, but no-one pays the slightest attention. The re-education efforts feels half-hearted. For Kyiv, the real focus is on using these PoWs as swaps to bring its own soldiers home. But when it comes to negotiating exchange lists, it turns out the men from the Donbas are a low priority for Russia. "Only a dozen or so have been transferred this year," Konstantin complains. "It seems like they don't want to exchange us. I think we will be the last to go." https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: DUBLIN — Ukraine wants European countries to reopen the debate over frozen Russian state assets, suggesting a partial disbursement and broader guarantees could help break the deadlock with Belgium, which vetoed the plan in December . Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov said the country was discussing several options with European partners to cover gaps in its defense and civilian budgets. Front-loading part of the EU’s €90 billion loan for Ukraine could help, he said, but would not be the only solution. “We are looking also to the opportunities in the EU and we suggest, in particular, the idea of the frozen assets,” Chentsov said on the sidelines of an informal meeting of European affairs ministers in Dublin on Friday. “It’s a smart way to generate money and cover the debt.” Advertisement Advertisement Using Russia's immobilized state assets to help fund Ukraine returned to the EU agenda after the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden last month called on the European Commission to explore “new options” for unlocking them. More than €200 billion in Russian central-bank assets are immobilized across the EU, with most held by Belgian-based financial depository Euroclear. The Belgian government has resisted proposals to use the funds, citing the potential legal and financial risks it could face in the event of Russian retaliation or litigation. Kyiv’s renewed appeal reflects the growing pressure to find additional money for Ukraine, with the country facing a substantial budget shortfall and Russia's full-scale invasion in its fifth year. The EU and Ukraine "need to consider other options, to consider, say, different figures as a first step" to get at least some of the Russian assets released, Chentsov said in response to a question from POLITICO about how Belgium might change its mind. Europe also needs new ideas about "how to guarantee this instrument," he added. "Maybe not only EU, but other players can step in and help to answer the concerns of Belgium. So it's important to start working again on the issue and look for the solution. "I'm sure that if we want to find a solution, we will find a solution," he added. Advertisement Advertisement But Belgium appears unmoved. “Our position remains the same," a spokesperson for Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot told POLITICO. The European Commission last addressed the frozen assets issue Monday, with chief spokesperson Paula Pinho saying Brussels was focused on disbursing the money from the EU's €90 billion loan for Ukraine. A Commission official said that position still holds. Camille Gijs contributed to this report.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: At the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian View image in fullscreen At the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian UK news Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community The men were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar Hannah Al-Othman and Vikram Dodd Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.46 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 17.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community. Rahman Salehi, 35, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism. Police say the two men wanted to use an improvised explosive device to carry out their attack. In a statement, counter-terrorism police (CTP) said the charges will allege they used “encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”. Furthermore the charges allege they obtained video instructions on how to make an IED, and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED. The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for CTP, said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.” She added: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran. While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.” The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. They were arrested in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of the city centre, before being held in custody at a London police station. Counter-terrorism police had been given more time to question the men, who were detained under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors. “This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue. “The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.” Salehi and Ahmadyan They are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October. Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “We have decided to prosecute Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan following a fast-paced counter-terrorism policing investigation in Greater Manchester in September targeting the Jewish community. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial. “We understand that this case may cause concern, particularly considering the arrests came on the eve of Yom Kippur. We want to assure the Jewish community that working with the police, their safety and that of the wider public is our highest priority.” The Metropolitan police, who are leading the investigation, said searches had also been carried out at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford. At the time of the arrests, Evans said police officers were “doing everything we can to keep them [the Jewish community] and the wider public safe”, while counter-terrorism police and local forces were working together “to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period”. Last year, Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by armed police after launching a terror attack during Yom Kippur at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester. Two men were killed during the attack, Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, while three others were injured.
